title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Exceptions
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document consolidates Redwood Inference's operational security and compliance guidance for RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, the secure SDLC, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for engineers, security reviewers, legal/compliance, and platform operators.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood-hosted services (hosted API, dedicated, private), control plane components, and customer-facing consoles and tools.

Ownership and Contacts

- Security (owner): security@redwood.com (primary contact)
- Platform (secondary): eng-platform@redwood.com
- SRE / Logging: eng-sre@redwood.com
- Evidence & Audit Coordinator: compliance@redwood.com

Version & Revision History

- 2025-11-01: Created by Jordan Lee (initial published guidance)
- 2026-03-04: Updated retention schedules, exception process, and CI/CD gating (reviewers: Priya Natarajan, Ethan Cole, Marina Alvarez)

1) Principles and High-Level Requirements

- Least privilege by default: All access must be restricted to the minimum set of privileges required for a role or task.
- Auditability: Relevant events must be captured and retained per retention policy to support investigations and compliance audits.
- Data locality and minimization: Customer data must remain in the approved region; sensitive fields must be classified and minimized in logs.
- Secure-by-default SDLC: Security checks are mandatory gate steps for all production deploys.

2) RBAC and Authentication

Goals: Enforce least-privilege access across control plane and infrastructure; provide auditable role assignments and periodic reviews.

Roles & Definitions (examples):
- system:internal-service — Non-human service accounts used by platform components (must be scoped to a single service).
- platform-admin — Full control of Redwood Console and infra for operational support (approved for small set of SRE/Platform members).
- security-auditor — Read-only access to logs, dashboards, and compliance evidence.
- customer-admin — Tenant-scoped admin for Dedicated/Private deployments with no cross-tenant visibility.

Role assignment rules:
1. All human accounts must use SSO (OIDC) backed by the corporate identity provider. MFA required for interactive access.
2. Service accounts must use short-lived tokens (rotated by the platform's token service) and be scoped to named resources.
3. Use attribute-based access where possible (team, environment, region).
4. All role grants require an explicit approval (ticket) recorded in the entitlement system.

Sample IAM policy snippet (control plane RBAC model):

```
{
  "principal": "group:eng-platform",
  "effect": "allow",
  "actions": ["deploy:create", "deploy:rollback", "runbook:execute"],
  "resources": ["project:api-gateway", "project:runtime-manager"]
}
```

Periodic review:
- Owners must review role memberships quarterly. Security will run quarterly entitlement reports and notify owners with stale or excessive privileges.

3) Authentication & Credential Management

- SSO/OIDC is mandatory for all human access; account provisioning is automated through HR integrations.
- KMS-backed key management for all encryption keys; HSM for production KMS keys used to encrypt customer secrets in Private deployments.
- Secrets must be stored in the approved secret store (Vault or cloud KMS secret manager). No plaintext secrets in code or logs.

4) Audit Logging

Scope: Audit logs must capture authentication events, RBAC changes (grants/revokes), administrative actions (deploys, config changes), data access to sensitive stores, and system-level errors that could indicate security-relevant behavior.

Minimum event set:
- auth.login (success/failure), auth.token.create, auth.token.revoke
- rbac.grant, rbac.revoke, rbac.role.create, rbac.role.delete
- deploy.start, deploy.complete, deploy.rollback
- data.access.read, data.access.write (with resource ID and principal)
- sys.config.change, sys.privilege.escalation

Logging architecture and storage:
- Agents forward structured JSON events to AuditLogService (internal Kafka topic `audit.events`), which is consumed by the Audit Pipeline for enrichment and long-term storage in the read-only audit lake (S3, encrypted with KMS).
- Real-time aggregation and SIEM integration: Events are forwarded to the SIEM (Splunk/Chronicle) for alerting and retention indexing.

Retention & SLOs:
- Audit logs retention: 7 years for compliance-critical events; default 2 years for operational events. See Data Retention table below for classification.
- Audit ingestion SLA: 99.9% of events must be available in the audit lake within 5 minutes.
- Alerting: Missing ingestion or pipeline backpressure will create P1 alert routed to oncall SRE and security.

Sensitive data redaction:
- PII and secrets must be redacted at the producer; log processors will apply additional redaction heuristics.

5) Data Residency and Retention

Purpose: Ensure customer data resides only in approved regions and is retained or deleted according to regulatory and contractual obligations.

Data classes and retention (summary):
- Customer Content (model inputs/outputs): Default retention 90 days; can be configured per customer contract. For customers requiring longer retention for audit, retention is set in the tenancy config and documented in the contract.
- Audit & Control Plane Events: 7 years (compliance-critical).
- Operational Metrics & Aggregates: 2 years.
- Backups & Snapshots: 1 year unless otherwise specified.

Region controls:
- All production data is tagged with region (us-east1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1). Cross-region replication occurs only where explicitly provisioned and authorized.
- Private deployment packages default to on-prem or VPC-resident storage; control plane access is mediated by approved tunnels or customer-managed endpoints.

Deletion and erasure workflow:
1. Data deletion requests are initiated via the Console or API, which creates a deletion ticket in the DataOps queue.
2. DataOps runs a pre-check for retention constraints (legal hold, pending audits).
3. If clear, DataOps schedules a deletion job that removes primary and replicated copies and verifies deletion via checksums.
4. An audit record is written to audit.events indicating deletion outcome.

6) Secure SDLC Requirements

Gates & tooling:
- Mandatory pre-merge checks: static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning (OSS vulnerabilities), linting, and unit tests.
- Build-time secrets scan to block PRs with leaked secrets.
- At merge to main: integration tests and dynamic analysis (DAST) for public endpoints.
- Pre-production: security regressions must be run against a curated eval suite; quality/security regressions block rollouts.

CI/CD policies:
- Production deploys require: approved change ticket, passing security gate, canary plan, and owner sign-off.
- Automated canary rollback: if error rate or latency SLOs breach threshold during canary, deploy is rolled back automatically.

Dependency & supply chain controls:
- Approved packages list and SBOM generation are required for release artifacts.
- Any new build-time or runtime dependency must be risk-assessed and documented.

Developer onboarding checklist (security items):
- Enroll in SSO & MFA; request team group membership via Access Request workflow.
- Complete secure-coding training (annual).
- Verify local dev environment uses the approved secret store and test credentials.

7) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Incident classification:
- P0: Confirmed production data breach or exfiltration affecting customers. Immediate page to Security + Execs.
- P1: Severe availability impacting incident with potential security implications. Page Security + SRE.
- P2: Contained incidents requiring investigation; notify Security.

Playbook summary (for security incidents):
1. Triage & Containment: Identify impacted systems and isolate network segments or revoke tokens as needed.
2. Evidence Preservation: Snapshot relevant hosts, preserve logs (immutable copy), and capture timeline entries in the incident tracker.
3. Notification: Follow internal notification matrix and external disclosure requirements (customers, regulators) per legal guidance.
4. Eradication & Recovery: Apply fixes, rotate credentials, rebuild compromised systems, validate via red-team tests.
5. Post-Incident Review: Root cause analysis, action items, SLO reassessments, and follow-up audits. Publish a redacted postmortem within 7 business days.

Immediate containment checklist (example):
- Revoke suspicious tokens (Auth Token Service).
- Isolate affected instances via firewall rules and ASG scaling actions.
- Suspend cross-tenant replication if data exfiltration suspected.
- Disable external access keys until rotated.

Evidence handling:
- Immutable copies of logs and host snapshots must be stored in the secure evidence bucket (read-only to investigators). Access to evidence is logged and limited to the incident response team and legal.

8) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Audit intake process:
- Trigger: Audit request received (internal or external).
- Compliance coordinator creates an evidence collection ticket and assigns owners.
- Owners collect artifacts: architecture diagrams, SLO/SLA docs, RBAC reports, audit logs, policy docs, penetration test reports, and change records.

Artifact catalogue (minimum):
- RBAC: entitlement exports (CSV), role definitions, approval tickets, and quarterly review logs.
- Audit Logs: relevant event exports with verification checksums and storage proofs.
- SDLC: SBOM, CI/CD run logs showing security gate passes, SAST/DAST reports.
- Incident History: redacted incident reports and remediation evidence.

Packaging & sign-off:
- Evidence packet is assembled in Evidence Vault (read-only folder per audit), digitally signed by Security and Compliance, and timestamped.
- For external audits, Compliance leads coordinate live sessions and provide read-only console views when required.

9) Risk and Exceptions

When exceptions are permitted:
- Exceptions are rare and granted only when a documented technical constraint or explicit customer contractual need exists.
- Temporary exceptions must have an expiration (max 90 days) and a compensating control (e.g., scoped monitoring, additional network segmentation).

Exception request process:
1. Submit exception request in the Risk & Exceptions tracker with: justification, owner, impact, compensating controls, and proposed expiration.
2. Security performs risk assessment; Compliance/legal consulted for regulatory impact.
3. Approval matrix:
   - Low risk: Security review + Platform owner
   - Medium risk: Security + Head of Platform + Compliance
   - High risk: Security + CISO + Legal + CTO
4. Approved exceptions are timeboxed and subject to weekly reviews until remediation is implemented.

Monitoring & enforcement:
- Exception inventory is published weekly. Automated checks will flag resources operating under exceptions for elevated telemetry and weekly security reviews.

10) Operational Runbooks & Playbooks (quick links)

Appendix A — Examples & CLI snippets

Export RBAC membership (example):
```
# Export group members to CSV
rcli iam export --group eng-platform --format csv > eng-platform-members.csv
```

Generate an evidence package (example):
```
evidence-cli collect --scope rbac,logs,sbom --since 2026-01-01 --output /evidence/package-2026-03-04.zip
```

Appendix B — Glossary

- Audit Lake: read-only long-term store for enriched audit events.
- Evidence Vault: access-controlled evidence repository used for audits.
- SBOM: Software Bill of Materials.
